cues.text: Gutenberg's Invention
Johann Gutenberg , a goldsmith and craftsman from Mainz, spent years developing movable metal type, oil-based printing ink, and a specially adapted press.
Together, these technologies made mechanical mass reproduction of text possible for the first time in the West.
Working largely in secret to protect his invention, Gutenberg partnered with the financier Johann Fust to fund the costly undertaking.
Choosing the Vulgate
For his first great work, Gutenberg chose the most important text he could print: the Latin Vulgate , St. Jerome's translation that had served as the Bible of the Western Church for a thousand years.

The resulting 42-line Bible , so named for the number of lines per column, is renowned even today for its beauty, using two elegantly designed Gothic type styles that mimicked the finest contemporary manuscript hands.
Printing the First Bible
Work on the Bible began around 1452 and was substantially complete by 1455; the future Pope Pius II reported having seen printed pages displayed at Frankfurt as early as March 1455.

Of the roughly 180 copies originally produced, some printed on vellum and most on paper, around forty-nine survive today in whole or substantial part, among the most treasured artifacts in the history of the book.
A Financial and Legal Struggle
The Bible's enormous cost led to a legal dispute between Gutenberg and his financial backer Fust, who sued for repayment.
A court ruling in 1455 stripped Gutenberg of much of his press and materials, even as the work he had begun was completed.
Despite this personal setback, Gutenberg continued printing other works, including an important Psalter, before his death around 1467-68.
Printing Spreads Across Europe
Within a generation, printing presses modeled on Gutenberg's techniques spread rapidly through German cities and then across the whole of Europe.

They drove down the cost of books, standardized texts (including subsequent editions of the Vulgate itself), and enabled far wider circulation of Scripture, sermons, papal documents, and eventually the polemical pamphlets of the Reformation.
Legacy
The Gutenberg Bible stands as the opening act of the printing revolution, arguably the single most consequential communications technology before the internet.

It transformed how Scripture, theology, and Church teaching circulated, made possible the rapid spread of both Catholic devotional literature and, within decades, the reforming and dissenting movements that would divide Western Christendom.
